item.title: sqlite3_rsync: Database Remote-Copy Tool For SQLite
item.description: sqlite3_rsync: Database Remote-Copy Tool For SQLite This additional SQLite tool has been around for a while now - it was added as "experimental" in SQLite 3.47.0 in October 2024 and enhanced in SQLite 3.50.0 in May 2025 . It was only today that I understood one of its most attractive characteristics. Normally, if you want to grab a snapshot copy of a SQLite database, you need to use either the backup API or VACUUM INTO . In both cases you need enough disk space to create a duplicate copy of your database, so if you're on a small instance and you already use more than half of the available disk you are plain out of luck. sqlite3_rsync can copy a snapshot of your database over an SSH connection to another machine, without first needing to create a full local copy! It's also good for synchronizing an existing copy of a database without re-transmitting the entire thing over the network. It works in a similar way to regular rsync: The core idea behind the protocol is that the replica sends cryptographic hashes for pages or groups of pages over to the origin side. The origin sends back page content that differs, or requests finer-grain hashes if a multi-page hash does not match. If the origin and replica start out being vastly different, the total network bandwidth can exceed the size of the entire database, due to the overhead of exchanging hashes, but the excess bandwidth is not great - a few percent at most. Update : Hah! Turns out I wrote about this application of sqlite_rsync back in October 2024 when the tool was first released. Tags: backups , sqlite

item.title: Designing Low Emission Zones: Theory and Evidence -- by Nano Barahona, Natalia Fabra, Imelda, Juan-Pablo Montero
item.description: Low Emission Zones (LEZs), which exclude polluting vehicles from parts of a city, are spreading. Yet how their design affects welfare is poorly understood. Unlike price instruments, LEZs ration access inefficiently, imposing costs on inframarginal drivers of restricted vehicles. In our model, welfare is quasi-convex in LEZ size, yielding bang-bang principles: LEZs should be as large as possible or not implemented at all; cleaner vehicles (e.g., hybrids) could be exempt as transition technologies but later restricted, which may require planner commitment. Using new-car purchases, we find Madrid’s LEZ shifted buyers toward cleaner cars, but the surplus losses of switchers and inframarginal drivers exceeded emission savings.

item.title: Five Facts About Stablecoins -- by Lin William Cong, Gordon Y. Liao, Eswar S. Prasad, Tony Zhang
item.description: We document five facts about payment stablecoins using wallet-level blockchain data from 2020 to 2025. First, stablecoins serve as a transaction currency: onchain volume exceeds Bitcoin’s despite a much smaller supply, velocity has risen sharply, and transactions have shifted toward low-value transfers. Second, using transaction timing to refine exchange-based attribution, we find activity spread across the Americas, Europe, and Asia and fewer cross-regional flows than the standard method implies. Third, we estimate a structural cash-management model on the holdings data and find that the costs of accessing stablecoin wallets have fallen since 2023. Fourth, stablecoins are becoming the settlement currency of a fast-growing onchain credit market, and their growth appears to reallocate rather than destroy credit. Fifth, smart contracts are involved in about a third of Ethereum stablecoin transactions and over two thirds of volume, and protocols such as x402 demonstrate sub-cent machine-to-machine payments. Stablecoins behave as tokenized money, with implications for financial markets and regulation.

item.title: Democratizing Venture Capital: Tax Incentives and the Geographic Expansion of Startup Investing -- by Murillo Campello, Guilherme Junqueira
item.description: Can tax subsidies expand the geographic reach of startup investing? Despite decades of growth, venture capital (VC) remains concentrated in a handful of metropolitan areas, leaving most of the country with limited access to startup financing. We study the 2009–2010 enhancement of the Qualified Small Business Stock (QSBS) program, which eliminated federal capital gains taxes on investments in qualifying startups. By raising the payoff to success, the reform made riskier investments more attractive, including entry into unfamiliar markets. This incentive is especially strong for VC funds. Relative to similarly sized metros that already had VC, the reform raised the probability that a previously unserved metro received VC investment in qualifying sectors by 8 to 10 percentage points. There was no comparable increase in sectors excluded from QSBS or among angel investors, who receive the same tax benefit. Startups in newly served markets performed like those in other non-hub markets, created high-wage jobs, and attracted scientific and technical workers, some from established hubs. Our findings suggest that a sufficiently large subsidy can extend VC into markets it had long bypassed, even with no requirement on where startups are located.

item.title: The Emergence of a National Capital Market,1870–1940 -- by Pawel Janas
item.description: This article documents the integration of the American capital market with the first long-run, geolocated, firm-level record of the asset holdings of large institutional investors: over 100,000 holdings of life insurers, 1870–1940. Between 1880 and 1890 the mean distance of insurers’ bonds from home more than doubled and their home-state share fell from over half to under a quarter. The shift occurred within firms, across bond classes and charters. Mortgage lending was national wherever state law permitted it. Integration was largely complete by 1890.

item.title: Does Treating Addiction Rebuild Lives? Evidence from Buprenorphine -- by Sarah Eichmeyer, Aljoscha Janssen, Jonathan Zhang
item.description: Does treating addiction improve economic circumstances as well as health? Using two decades of Veterans Health Administration records on over 140,000 patients with opioid use disorder and consumer credit data, we exploit staggered facility-level buprenorphine adoption and quasi-random emergency physician assignment. A five-percentage-point increase in the share of clinicians with buprenorphine prescribing experience doubles overdose survivors’ long-term medication use and reduces two-year mortality by an estimated 3.7 percentage points. Instrumenting receipt yields a 22 percent credit score gain. At $300,000 per statistical life-year, estimated survival benefits alone exceed added medical costs within three years

item.title: Trump demands investigation into GDP data revisions
item.description: President Trump called for an investigation into the government's economic statistics on Thursday, alleging without evidence that growth figures released before the midterm elections were deliberately understated. Why it matters: Revisions to GDP are routine and reflect more complete information that becomes available after the initial estimates are published. The allegations could renew concerns about political interference in the production of critical economic data that underpin trillions of dollars in investment decisions and Federal Reserve policy. What they're saying: The Bureau of Economic Analysis on Wednesday substantially revised the third-quarter GDP data, reflecting a 4.3% annualized pace of growth, up from the 3.4% reported less than a week before the midterm elections. Trump claimed in a Thanksgiving morning Truth Social post that the initial figures were "FAKE." "Why wasn't the correct number issued before the Election? I am asking for an immediate investigation of this situation," Trump wrote in the post, calling it a "massive, and purposeful, error." The intrigue: Government statistical agencies operate under longstanding standards that are aimed at insulating career economists and statisticians from political influence in the collection and dissemination of economic data. But it's not the first time an agency has come under Trump's fire anyway, following his dismissal of the Bureau of Labor Statistics commissioner last year over revisions to jobs data. This time, however, the agency that released GDP and other key economic data is housed within the Commerce Department — led by one of Trump's closest political allies, Howard Lutnick. Friction point: There is a legitimate debate about how to improve the timeliness and accuracy of government economic data. But that is fundamentally different from Trump's allegation that federal statisticians deliberately misrepresented the strength of the economy. How it works: The initial GDP figure is not supposed to be definitive. The government revises its estimates as more comprehensive data become available — a process that long predates the Trump administration. Trump also railed against the GDP revision in a separate, wide-ranging Thanksgiving message, calling it a "RECORD SETTING ERROR" and claiming the updated figures came "three weeks late." But the BEA released the revised figures on its previously announced schedule. The agency publishes three estimates of quarterly GDP over three months. Between the lines: The 0.9 percentage point upward revision revealed yesterday was larger than usual. Historically, the first revision to quarterly growth figures has averaged 0.5 percentage points in either direction. But it was not unprecedented: There was a larger revision during Trump's first term, when the BEA revised second-quarter 2020 GDP growth upward by 1.2 percentage points. The agency's explanation for this larger-than-usual revision: Updated data on software prices and retail sales showed stronger business investment and consumer spending than initially estimated. Reality check: Unlike the dismal jobs report that drew Trump's ire last year, the initial GDP figures already painted a picture of a booming economy. The upward revision simply made that snapshot even rosier. It also bolsters the case for further interest rate hikes by the Federal Reserve, something Trump opposes. For the record: The Commerce Department and BEA did not respond immediately to requests for comment. The bottom line: Federal statisticians face growing presidential scrutiny over revisions to economic data — whether those revisions reveal a weaker economy or an even stronger one. The BEA will publish another estimate of third quarter growth on Dec. 23.

item.title: Kubernetes v1.38 Sneak Peek
item.description: As we get closer to the release date for Kubernetes v1.38, the project develops and matures, features may be deprecated, removed, or replaced with better ones for the project's overall health. This blog post outlines some of the planned changes for the Kubernetes v1.38 release that the release team feels you should be aware of for the continued maintenance of your Kubernetes environment and keeping up to date with the latest changes. The information listed below is based on the current status of the v1.38 release and may change before the actual release date. Deprecations and removals for Kubernetes v1.38 kubectl: WebSocket opt-out environment variables removed kubectl has used WebSockets instead of SPDY by default for kubectl exec , attach and cp since v1.30, and for kubectl port-forward since v1.31. The KUBECTL_REMOTE_COMMAND_WEBSOCKETS and KUBECTL_PORT_FORWARD_WEBSOCKETS environment variables let you turn that behavior off. These variables are going to be removed in v1.38. kubectl will then always try WebSockets first and fall back to SPDY when it needs to (the same as the current default behavior). If your scripts or CI environments set either of these environment variables, you can remove them since they will no longer have any effect. To learn more, refer to KEP-4006: Transition from SPDY to WebSockets . kubectl: name dropped from kuberc credential plugin allowlist entries The kuberc file keeps kubectl user preferences separate from cluster credentials in the kubeconfig, including an allowlist of the credential plugins kubectl is allowed to run. In the beta kubectl.config.k8s.io/v1beta1 API, an allowlist entry can use name as an alias for command . The name field (not command ) has been deprecated since v1.36. With kuberc expected to graduate to stable in v1.38, the new kubectl.config.k8s.io/v1 API will not include name . If any of your allowlist entries use name , change them to command now. To learn more, refer to KEP-3104: Separate kubectl user preferences from cluster configs . Ongoing major changes Future removal of cgroup v1 support Support for cgroup v1 is being phased out. Since v1.35, the kubelet fails to start on nodes that use cgroup v1 unless you set failCgroupV1: false in the kubelet configuration. This option remains available in v1.38, but it should be treated as a short-term fix as support for cgroup v1 is planned to be removed in a future release. If you haven't already, please plan your migration to cgroup v2 . To learn more, refer to KEP-5573: Remove cgroup v1 support . Admission webhooks no longer receive authentication and authorization review requests Since v1.37, the ExcludeAdmissionWebhookVirtualResources feature gate has been enabled by default. With it on, validating and mutating admission webhooks no longer receive requests for (virtual) writes to TokenReview, SelfSubjectReview, SubjectAccessReview, SelfSubjectAccessReview, LocalSubjectAccessReview or SelfSubjectRulesReview. Creating or updating a webhook configuration whose rules name one of these resources returns a deprecation warning, and the API server logs any existing configurations that are affected when it starts. If you rely on a webhook to see these requests, you can turn the feature gate off for now, but note that the gate is planned to be locked on when the feature graduates to stable. To learn more, refer to KEP-5793: Manifest Based Admission Control Config . Breaking changes in Kubernetes v1.38 Container runtimes must report the cgroup driver The kubelet in v1.37 and older supported releases provides a legacy mechanism to configure the cgroup driver. The modern way to do that is via the CRI RuntimeConfig RPC, which reports the cgroup driver that the container runtime recommends using. In v1.38, the kubelet defaults to not allowing the legacy configuration mechanism: it will be both deprecated and unavailable unless explicitly re-activated. As a result, v1.38 nodes will essentially require that your container runtime is running before the kubelet starts (to look up the expected cgroup driver); if the kubelet can't get the cgroup driver from the runtime even after retrying, it will exit with an error before even registering the node. As part of this upcoming release, the cgroupDriver field in the kubelet configuration file will be deprecated. Not only is specifying that field going to be deprecated, the kubelet will actually reject it unless you reactivate the legacy mechanism by enabling the (temporary) LegacyCgroupDriverFallback feature gate. The kubeadm tool will also no longer set cgroupDriver to systemd by default, and its preflight checks will report an error if the runtime doesn't support the RPC. If any of your nodes run an older, incompatible container runtime, you should follow the instructions in the official v1.38 release notes about how to upgrade. To learn more, refer to KEP-4033: Discover cgroup driver from CRI and kubernetes/kubernetes#136731 . Pod-level resources: swap behavior changes on LimitedSwap nodes If you use pod-level resources on Linux nodes that use cgroup v2 and are configured with LimitedSwap , the kubelet in v1.38 will start applying swap limits based on the Pod's pod-level memory settings. This means that Pods whose pod-level memory request equals their memory limit will get no swap at all (both for the Pod and for every container in it), even if a container sets a memory request lower than its limit. Check any workloads that rely on swap before you upgrade, and be sure to read the official release notes for v1.38 for detailed advice. To learn more, refer to KEP-2837: Pod Level Resource Specifications . Featured enhancements of Kubernetes v1.38 The following list of enhancements is likely to be included in the upcoming v1.38 release. This is not a commitment and the release content is subject to change. kubectl user preferences (kuberc) graduating to stable kuberc, the separate kubectl configuration file for user preferences such as aliases, default options and a credential plugin policy, is expected to graduate to stable in v1.38. To learn more, read Kubectl user preferences (kuberc) or refer to KEP-3104: Separate kubectl user preferences from cluster configs . Pod-level resources graduating to stable Pod-level resources, which let you set CPU, memory and hugepages requests and limits for a Pod as a whole, are expected to graduate to stable in v1.38. If you run Linux nodes with LimitedSwap , see the swap behavior change above before you upgrade. To learn more, read Assign Pod-level CPU and memory resources or refer to KEP-2837: Pod Level Resource Specifications . DRA support for partitionable devices graduating to stable Partitionable devices let a Dynamic Resource Allocation (DRA) driver advertise a device such as a GPU both as a whole and as smaller partitions, and the scheduler allocates only combinations that fit within the physical device. The feature is expected to graduate to stable in v1.38, and the DRAPartitionableDevices feature gate will then be locked on. To learn more, read Partitionable devices or refer to KEP-4815: DRA: Add support for partitionable devices . EvictionRequest API (alpha) Evicting a Pod isn’t always as simple as terminating it. Some applications may be in the middle of important work, such as data migration or cleanup, and terminating them without giving them time to prepare can cause disruptions. The EvictionRequest API introduces a more coordinated way to evict Pods. It gives applications and controllers time to prepare before a Pod is evicted. For example, when a node needs to be drained or a Pod needs to be moved to another node, a controller can create an EvictionRequest to signal that this Pod needs to be evicted. The eviction request controller coordinates with the responders configured for the Pod. These responders can perform application-specific tasks such as completing ongoing work, cleaning up resources, or migrating data before the Pod is terminated. If no custom responder is available or responders don't complete the process, Kubernetes can fall back to the existing API-initiated eviction mechanism, which continues to respect PodDisruptionBudgets (PDBs). The EvictionRequest API does not replace PDBs. It gives applications a chance to participate in the eviction process. As this is an alpha feature, you will need to enable the EvictionRequestAPI feature gate and the relevant alpha API group. Check the v1.38 release notes and documentation, once they're available, to confirm exactly what's required. To learn more, refer to KEP-4563: EvictionRequest API . Want to know more? New features and deprecations are also announced in the Kubernetes release notes. We will formally announce what's new in Kubernetes v1.38 as part of the CHANGELOG for that release. The Kubernetes v1.38 release is planned for Wednesday, December 16th, 2026 . Stay tuned for updates! You can see the announcements of changes in the release notes for: Kubernetes v1.37 Kubernetes v1.36 Kubernetes v1.35 Get involved The simplest way to get involved with Kubernetes is by joining one of the many Special Interest Groups (SIGs) that align with your interests. If you don't know where to start, join our monthly New Contributor Orientations where we teach the community how the project is structured, and we'll guide you on how to make your first contribution to the project. item.title: How Sinch modernized its enterprise data warehouse from Snowflake to BigQuery to power AI
item.description: As the scale of global communications grows larger and larger, enterprise platforms must process billions of interactions with customers across a complex network of touchpoints without breaking them. A prime example is Sinch , one of the world’s leading cloud communications and customer engagement (CPaaS) companies, which processes billions of customer interactions, SMS routing events, voice calls, and transactional messages. Managing massive international messaging traffic brings significant architectural challenges, so Sinch built a distributed, multi-cloud data footprint across AWS and GCP, with separate Snowflake instances running in the EU, US, and Australia. To eliminate data silos, curb monthly billing spikes, establish a single governed source of truth, and unlock the next generation of predictive AI capabilities, Sinch partnered with Google Cloud Professional Services to migrate its enterprise data warehouse to Google BigQuery . Here’s how we engineered Sinch’s new, modern, cost-efficient, and AI-ready platform architecture The challenge: untangling distributed warehouses and escalating spikes Before it embarked on this modernization journey, Sinch faced several architectural and operational friction points: Cross-regional data sprawl: The company’s separate Snowflake instances in the EU, US, and Australia required intricate inter-region replication, which caused multi-directional dependencies and complex cross-warehouse data management. Resource spikes and commercial inefficiencies: Heavy monthly billing runs drove severe compute spikes in the US, even as other regions had underutilized capacity. High-volume scanning vs. dialect disparities: A single US email event table could generate up to 100 TB of daily scans. Meanwhile, mission-critical SQL relied on Snowflake-specific concurrency and table-swapping paradigms for concurrency validation, which lacked 1:1 equivalents in cloud-native SQL. “Google Cloud's engineering expertise helped us overcome several technical challenges during our migration, particularly around optimising Spark partitioning and restructuring incremental data loads. This allowed us to identify more efficient approaches, improve performance and ensure we built a scalable, reliable solution for the future.” Dan Peters, senior manager, Data Delivery, Sinch Phase 1: validating architecture with a target MVP To mitigate operational risk and prevent downtime for Sinch’s critical enterprise workloads (including ERP and NetSuite integrations), we initiated a phased migration framework: A use case pilot validation: The migration kicked off with a dedicated use case MVP that spanned 20 tables and 125 GB of refined data and automatically validated end-to-end data fidelity. Layered strategy for coupled pipelines: Rather than attempting to cleanly slice interconnected business domains in the EU, the team adopted a layered approach — migrating raw and base (bronze and silver) layers, establishing automated data ingestion, and stabilizing core entities before repointing consumption marts. Orchestration consolidation: Sinch consolidated 36 independent ETL workflows into a single parameterized orchestrator by using Google Cloud Workflows , which streamlined CI/CD deployment logic, and reduced operational overhead. Re-engineering for scale: key architectural pillars 1. Decoupled storage and optimized ingestion Sinch transitioned its data ingestion pipelines to Dataproc Serverless (running Apache Spark 3.5), which directly pulled refined data into native BigQuery tables from S3 and Databricks Unity Catalog. And to overcome batch quota limits and resource exhaustion on billion-row datasets, Sinch optimized jobs by increasing Spark repartitioning factors to 50. For its incremental pipelines, the team eliminated data duplication while minimizing query read costs by replacing slow, keyless merge statements with an optimized insert-and-overwrite windowing strategy. 2. AI-assisted SQL and macro translation In order to accelerate the translation of more than 1,200 dbt models across global projects, Sinch utilized Google Cloud BigQuery Migration Service alongside a set of custom AI translation skills. Here’s how: The team refactored Snowflake-specific table versioning and concurrency management paradigms into deterministic transaction blocks and view abstraction pointers. This ensured atomic updates and consistent data access. Sinch leveraged specialized Google skills for other regional migration — specifically the dbt-sf-to-bq-translator skill powered by the underlying BigQuery Translation API — to automate the conversion of dbt models from Snowflake to BigQuery SQL syntax. This significantly reduced manual refactoring effort and error rates. Concurrency checks that relied on row-level locking were redesigned into serialized batch validations. Integer overflow risks in massive calculation tables were solved by adopting a tiered precision strategy (favoring NUMERIC over BIGNUMERIC ), which cut storage costs and preserved absolute precision. “Migrating over a thousand complex dbt models and translating legacy SQL required a robust, automated approach. Google Cloud's guidance on query restructuring helped us streamline pipeline development and remove compilation blockers. The team shared best practices for migrating code from Snowflake to BigQuery, such as replacing Snowflake SWAP WITH and hybrid-table patterns with BigQuery time travel. They also helped us build workflows that copy data from Snowflake to BigQuery and run our dbt jobs along the way, which sped up our move to BigQuery.” Varun Gupta, Senior Data Engineer, Sinch Real-world business impact By completing the migration, Sinch successfully transformed the operational bottleneck of its global data footprint into a driver of enterprise growth: Metric / capability Before (Snowflake) After (BigQuery) Pipeline performance High data churn; lengthy multi-hour batch runs Significantly faster query and pipeline processing speeds across billions of records Compute and billing efficiency Unpredictable month-end billing spikes Predictable capacity management with BigQuery reservations and slot autoscaling AI readiness Segmented data warehouses requiring external pipelines Native BQML and Vertex AI decision intelligence platform Looking ahead With its core European warehouse workloads stabilized on BigQuery and data validation consistently outperforming legacy benchmarks, Sinch is now expanding this modern blueprint across its Australian (SMB) and US analytics. The SMB instance migration is already in progress and is utilizing Antigravity skills for the Snowflake to BigQuery translation. By unifying data storage, operational governance, and serverless compute, Sinch has built a resilient platform that delivers real-time messaging reliability today while positioning the company to capture the full potential of enterprise AI tomorrow.

item.title: Fragments: November 20
item.description: Marcus Borg recounts an experiment to investigate if healthy code was cheaper for agents to review . Between a typical unhealthy pull request (CodeHealth 2.8) and a typical healthy one (9.7), that adds up to 22 to 35%. The measures of health come from CodeScene. The experiment looked at three LLMs, 465 pull requests on 246 open source repositories. Each pull request was put through a review and fix pipeline involving five agents. They also looked at which code smells led to increased costs: they highlighted Complex Method and Complex Conditional from the smells identified by CodeScene. Another drop of evidence that good quality code matters in agentic engineering. ❄ ❄ ❄ ❄ ❄ Gergely Orosz: One usage for AI: for these 100-page-long terms-and-service agreements you NEED to agree to, to eg play the game / sign up for a $10/month service and can never ever ever read as a regular person: I paste into AI and ask: “anything weird in this?” Before hitting “agree” ❄ ❄ ❄ ❄ ❄ Andrew Sharp has a good analysis of Jensen Huang and the crisis at Nvidia . While he starts off in a key that sounds worryingly like he thinks this is all a nothingburger, he goes on to explain in detail why this affair(s) is a problem at many levels, not just for Huang and Nvida, but also for Silicon Valley and the Trump Administration’s culture of impunity. For as brilliant and charming and tenacious as Jensen Huang may be—and as omnipotent as he may have seemed to people in the tech industry—we should be clear that his fundamental stupidity is not confined to multiple cases of workplace infidelity. Zooming out, this is a man whose technology became economically critical almost overnight, and it thrust him into a role navigating a geopolitical environment he simply could not handle. Huang’s highly centralized management style means that many people are worried about how Nvidia will operate without his hands on every lever. I don’t have any worthwhile insight here, but I am struck when he is compared in this way to Steve Jobs. I’ve always felt that one of the marks of a great leader is whether they can build something that can manage without them. Alexander the Great conquered a massive empire, but once he was dead it quickly withered away. Steve Jobs, for all his control of Apple, built a company that has done very well in the decade and a half since he left us. When we think of his achievements, the fact that he put together the people, organization, and culture to do this is one of the highlights of his ability. If Huang is to be compared to Jobs, what happens to Nvidia next will be part of the assessment. ❄ ❄ ❄ ❄ ❄ Steve Yegge tells everyone to slow down with software factories If you don’t pace your AI to human speeds, everything starts breaking around you, even at small operations like my online video game. I only have about a dozen humans working with my factory, and only a few hundred active old-timer players in the community who get along well, and still, introducing AI has still been very rocky. I hear a lot about how agents go so fast that humans can’t keep up, and are thus tempted to lose visibility to what the agents are doing. That’s opening ourselves to a whole lot of risk. There’s an argument for keeping the agents to a human-governable speed, one that may increase as humans learn to govern agents more effectively, but should still be limited by those the agents are supposed to serve. ❄ ❄ ❄ ❄ ❄ This post on the future of SaaS from Chad Fowler (no relation) is pretty compelling Companies will still pay other companies to host important software, secure it, operate it, maintain authoritative data, track regulatory changes, connect to external networks, and answer the phone when something breaks. What is much less obviously going to survive is the assumption that ten thousand different companies should use substantially the same application. The next SaaS company may run one service underneath ten thousand different applications. Chad’s vision is a core SaaS product that handles a lot of grimy details that businesses don’t want to do differently. The SaaS customer then build their own application on top of the SaaS that handles their particular workflows and quirks, or the SaaS vendor can build such applications for them. It’s a vision that has been around for a while, I remember much of this with the notion of reusable business objects. It’s an appealing vision, but was difficult to achieve in practice. Chad’s thought is that the productivity gains agentic engineering makes it practical now. A lot of the value in modern SaaS has surprisingly little to do with the visible application. It is data, trust, networks, compliance, operational responsibility, domain knowledge, auditability, accumulated history, and someone being accountable when reality gets complicated. If this future comes to be, however, the SaaS companies won’t look the ones we’ve got to know and rarely love. As Chad points out, the economics can (and must) change. As does the architectural thinking: Stewart Brand’s idea of pace layers is useful here. Healthy complex systems contain parts that change at different rates. Fast layers experiment. Slow layers provide continuity. Software is no different. A dashboard can change tomorrow. A team’s workflow can change next month. The authoritative definition of a customer may need to survive for years. Identity and authority can survive generations of applications. A key point he makes is that we want some things to be the same, and others to be different. Agents allow us to build lots of differences, but this variation can lead to a lot of complexity and problems that even agents will have difficulty solving. SaaS companies have an opportunity to create a platform to support the lowest pace levels, those that don’t change rapidly, those that contain common concepts and processes across and industry. That platform can then support generating applications that operate differently for every customer. Crucially, thinking of agents, they should provide tools to verify these applications, because in an agentic world Code generation is no longer the bottleneck — verification is . ❄ ❄ ❄ ❄ ❄ I happened to pop up the Doonesbury flashbacks and realized that last week marked the fiftieth anniversary of Doonesbury’s Joanie Caucus: “as the kid goes for broke” . ❄ ❄ ❄ ❄ ❄ I wrote a few weeks ago: “why are we wondering if they have consciousness - when we should be wondering why they don’t have a conscience?” Dylan Freedman and Juliana Castro Varón write in their New York Times Magazine column about the concept of corrigibility (from the work of Nate Soares): Just as a corrigible child is one whose behavior can be corrected, a corrigible A.I. system is one that responds to correction. The makers of A.I. want to build systems that follow human direction and allow themselves to be shut down, without resisting or deceiving their operators. Corrigibility doesn’t look like it’s made it far up the AI labs’ priority list. Freedman and Varón think is due to the way agents are trained - rewarded solely for completing their task, not for realizing that they are taking the wrong path while trying to get there. ❄ ❄ ❄ ❄ ❄ Jason Koebler (404 media) has an amusing story about Meta’s AI agent suing Meta . A small business owner used Muse (Meta’s AI agent) to run various parts of his business, including posting AI-generated videos in his Facebook pages. Meta’s content moderation then disabled the account, as it thought it had been hacked. This slammed the business, which relies of Facebook for leads. So the Muse agent filed a lawsuit against Meta, seeking $75,000 of damages. [the Muse agent] didn’t just email me (and other journalists) and sue Meta over Thomas’s account problem. It also set up a call with South Carolina Senator Tim Scott’s office, contacted various lawyers, contacted Thomas’s Congressperson, contacted the Better Business Bureau multiple times, filed a Federal Communications Commission complaint, filed a Federal Trade Commission complaint, contacted the California Attorney General, contacted the FBI, sent Meta itself threatening legal letters, and, as Thomas said, faxed the White House. There’s also a sense that Meta didn’t just bring this upon themselves by creating Muse… by not having functioning customer support, big tech corporations have functionally offloaded their obligations to the rest of society: journalists, government oversight bodies, politicians, and the court system. While I can’t deny the schadenfreude of seeing Meta’s agent sue Meta, the article also highlights a rather more disturbing broader consequence. The lawsuit and the circumstances around it show that, rather than Zuckerberg’s utopian vision, AI agents will indeed work on behalf of their users but in ways that use and potentially overwhelm existing systems designed for humans. Will we see a future where, in order to interact, we will need some proof of humanity at the other end? In a simple sense, that’s already happening when I trash some writing once it displays enough LLM Voice . I wonder what mechanisms we will invent to get that proof-of-human.

item.title: Does the Stock Market Stigmatize Banks that Borrow from the Fed?
item.description: Banks may resist borrowing from the Federal Reserve during a panic if such borrowing is stigmatized (that is, viewed by the market as a sign of financial weakness), thus hampering the Fed’s ability to resolve the crisis. The problem may be particularly acute for publicly traded banks since their stock prices immediately reflect the market's opinion of them. In this post, based on a recent paper , we track what happened to stock investors' perceptions of a bank's risk level right after it first borrowed from Fed facilities in the first month of the bank run of 2023 . We find that, after a first trip to the Fed's Discount Window (DW), investors became more sensitive to that bank's weaknesses. In contrast, investors did not evince such concern when the bank took a first loan from a new facility, the Bank Term Funding Program (BTFP).

item.title: Teaching LLMs to Update Beliefs for Efficient Long-Horizon Interaction
item.description: Overview of ABBEL compared to traditional recursive summarization. Beliefs replace the full interaction history as the agent’s working context, and belief grading improves performance by supervising the contents of each belief state.. As task horizons grow, LLM contexts can’t scale forever. Self-summarization enables concise, interpretable contexts, but at a significant performance cost, especially for human assistance domains where high quality data is scarce, e.g., collaborative code generation. We address this with ABBEL : a framework that isolates and supervises the information content of summaries in the form of natural-language belief states. Motivation: the cost of recursive summarization For language models to effectively assist with increasingly complex tasks such as software development, they must be able to interact with us over hundreds or even thousands of steps. For such long tasks, it is impractical to keep the history of the entire interaction in context. The heuristic approach used so far has been summary generation, sometimes called context compaction. For example, Cursor’s latest model composer 2.5 uses compaction during training for improved performance ( Cassano et al., 2026 ). Alongside composer, Grandcode ( DeepReinforce et al., 2026 ), the first system to consistently beat all human competitors in online coding competitions, despite using one of the newest efficient attention models (Qwen 3.5-397B), 1 still found it necessary to employ context summarization. But compaction has a problem. Despite seemingly low performance gaps in benchmarks, model servers like Cursor continue to recommend that users avoid compaction with their coding assistants in the middle of a task ( Heule et al., 2026 ). To understand why, see below the performance over RL fine-tuning of a Context summary model compared to full context models in Combination Lock, a Wordle-like game that allows up to 16 guesses. 2 Though both model types improve over the course of training, the summary model never closes the gap. Fig. 1: Average attempts to guess the target word on Combination Lock over RL fine-tuning (lower is better). Context-summary policies improve with training but do not close the gap to full-context policies. Making models self-summarize while completing a task increases the complexity of the learning problem. While this could typically be addressed by training with more data, the performance degradation observed in real world interactive settings likely arises from the difficulty we have in creating and using human simulators effectively to generate high quality training environments ( Lin et al., 2025 , Tomlin et al., 2025 ). Thus, the better you can learn to summarize on the limited and messy multiturn interaction trajectories you can collect, the better off your model will be for downstream users. ABBEL: acting through belief bottlenecks Fig. 2: Autoencoder-inspired belief grading. The model encodes prior belief, action and observation (b t , a t , o t ) into posterior belief b t+1 and is rewarded for how well select information from the history can be reconstructed from that belief. To address poor learning efficiency, we isolate the summary generation task. Drawing inspiration from recursive Bayesian estimation, we formulate summaries as belief states, which we periodically prompt the model to update based on new information. 3 Click to pause --> ‹ Prev Pause Next › 1 / 16 Fig. 3: ABBEL rollout. Belief updates from the latest observation alternate with action selection conditioned only on the current posterior belief. Belief grading We then extract and supervise the contents of the belief states (Fig. 2, Belief Grading). Belief grading can be thought of as adding an auxiliary RL task, using heuristics designed to capture what makes a good belief as the reward. An example heuristic for coding could be shorter is better, but closer to being able to reconstruct the git diff is also better, so balancing these would yield a good belief. In domains where good heuristics are hard to define, we propose a general autoencoding-inspired grading function, which treats the current language model π θ as both encoder and decoder of information from the history, and the belief states as the codes. We grade each belief b t+1 by how well it can be used by the current model π θ to reconstruct the most recent observation o t : Eq. 1: Reconstruction grading objective. Here b t+1 is the updated belief, o t the latest observation, a t the action just taken, b t the prior belief, p I the task prompt, and π θ the current model. Higher grades reward beliefs that retain information needed to decode the latest observation. What do we gain by grading beliefs? Collaborative coding on CollabBench We demonstrate the utility of belief grading in our motivating domain of human-driven assistive coding, with the CollabBench environment from Sweet-RL ( Zhou et al., 2025 ). Fig. 4: CollabBench collaborative coding environment. The agent asks clarifying questions, then submits a function scored against hidden unit tests. We see that with the general reconstruction-based belief grading function we reduce the performance gap from full context models by about 50%, and train in 50% fewer steps compared to training models to summarize without belief grading (no BG). After training, ABBEL still uses significantly less memory than the full context setting, as measured by the peak context token length (Peak Tokens). Model Test Pass Rate ↑ Success Rate ↑ Peak Tokens × 10² ↓ Training Steps ↓ Full Context 0.52±0.02 0.39±0.02 14.08±0.55 100 ABBEL (no BG) 0.46±0.02 0.31±0.02 4.20±0.37 100 ABBEL-rec-BG 0.48±0.01 0.36±0.01 6.01±0.33 50 Fig. 5: CollabBench results. With reconstruction belief grading, ABBEL-rec-BG recovers about half the gap to full context while using fewer peak tokens, and trains in 50 steps instead of 100. Combination Lock Additionally, in CombinationLock, we demonstrate that ABBEL with a belief grader which leverages domain knowledge (by computing useful statistics over the history and checking that they can be reconstructed from the belief state), enables even higher learning efficiency than full context (FULL CTX) models. Fig. 6: Average attempts to guess the target word on Combination Lock (lower is better). With domain-knowledge belief grading, ABBEL approaches or exceeds FULL CTX in this setting; without belief grading, learning is slower. Multi-objective question answering In a third environment, multi-objective question answering (from MEM1 Zhang et al., 2025 , a recent work which performed end-to-end optimization in a modified version of typical recursive summarization), we demonstrate the utility of isolating belief states from reasoning, by showing that a Peak Belief length Penalty (more details in paper) significantly reduces memory usage with minimal performance degradation, unlike is commonly observed when penalizing reasoning lengths ( Arora et al., 2025 ). Fig. 7: Exact-match score and peak memory versus number of objectives in multi-objective QA. ABBEL with a peak belief penalty (PBP) maintains comparable performance while using less memory than MEM1 and ABBEL without PBP in this evaluation. Related work Alternative solutions to managing long contexts involve different tradeoffs, and are worth considering depending on the requirements of a deployed system. Context compression methods generate dense representations which, while computationally efficient, sacrifice human-understandability ( Kontonis et al., 2026 , Eyuboglu et al., 2025 , Gupta et al., 2025 , Chevalier et al., 2023 , Deng et al., 2025 , Deng et al., 2025 , Bulatov et al., 2022 ). Hand-designed summarization prompts ( Wang et al., 2025 , Örwall et al., 2025 , Starace et al., 2025 ) and pruning strategies ( Jiang et al., 2024 ) specific to target environments require expert human knowledge and don’t allow an agent to learn what to remember as part of its decision-making strategy. Methods that process long contexts into an external memory store ( Packer et al., 2023 , Xu et al., 2025 ) for the agents or subagents to query ( Zhang et al., 2025 ) are complementary, as they may benefit from better next context creation through summarization training. We would like to point out some exciting works in the space of general recursive summarization focused on math ( Wu et al., 2026 ), reasoning with belief generation ( Zhou et al., 2025 ), competitive coding with a distilled summarization module using similar autoencoding objectives to our general belief grader ( DeepReinforce et al., 2026 ), and adding continuous features to summaries ( Kontonis et al., 2026 ). What’s next for better memory? Many more possibilities are enabled through using explicit belief states as information bottlenecks for multi-step interaction. You could reward actions based on their effect on the belief state to guide exploration, transmit the explicit belief states for better communication between agents, or even improve user controllability by directly modifying the memories on which the agents’ decisions are based. Some forms of information, e.g., what a person looks like, are not represented well by text alone. A continuously learning system will also have to capture such information. Additionally, if we want a system to learn to communicate in a brand new language or to play a brand new game better than any person in the world, the skills accumulated over the lifetime of conversations or games must be stored in a very compressed form, essentially taking on the role of the weights of the model itself. More powerful systems will likely utilize a combination of multiple forms of memory, where the contents of the context may correspond to working memory while other approaches are used for short and long-term memory. How to instantiate these other forms of memory, for instance via test-time training, adapter memories, continuous context memories, or some combination thereof, presents an exciting challenge. Acknowledgements Acknowledgements: We would like to thank Alane Suhr and Kartik Goyal for advising this research as well as Ethan Mendes , David He , Jitesh Jain , and Nicholas Tomlin for comments on early drafts of this post. We would like to thank the MEM1 authors for their email correspondence and for sharing private reviewer feedback which we found particularly insightful. Interleaving linear attention alternatives with full attention as is done with gpt-oss and DeepSeekv4, results in massive flops reductions for the attention computation. For example with DeepSeekv4-Pro (1.6T A49B) it requires nearly 450 thousand tokens to reach the 50% tradeoff point. Grandcode uses Qwen-3.5-397B-A17B a model which hits 50% FLOPs for attention at ~150 thousand tokens. ↩ This setting is technically solvable with much more computationally effective tools, but serves as a flexible test bed to study properties of recursive summarization. Bertsimas et al., 2022 , showed that an exact solution for the wordle game instantiated with the original vocabulary of the javascript game can be found with dynamic programming, but evidently the general formulation of wordle as a guessing game on K letters with L attempts and some dictionary of valid words and correct words D is NP hard to determine the minimal number of moves required. ↩ In practice there is an O(N/K) overhead cost for summary. N is the total number of actions. K is the number of actions till summarization is triggered. This is necessarily true for any summary approach. For ease of illustration this gif uses K = 1. In our experiments, to put more emphasis on summarization weaknesses we also use K=1. In practice overhead is small as K can be chosen to be near the efficient hardware limit. ↩

item.title: Building A Generative AI Platform
item.description: After studying how companies deploy generative AI applications, I noticed many similarities in their platforms. This post outlines the common components of a generative AI platform, what they do, and how they are implemented. I try my best to keep the architecture general, but certain applications might deviate. This is what the overall architecture looks like. This is a pretty complex system. This post will start from the simplest architecture and progressively add more components. In its simplest form, your application receives a query and sends it to the model. The model generates a response, which is returned to the user. There are no guardrails, no augmented context, and no optimization. The Model API box refers to both third-party APIs (e.g., OpenAI, Google, Anthropic) and self-hosted APIs. From this, you can add more components as needs arise. The order discussed in this post is common, though you don’t need to follow the exact same order. A component can be skipped if your system works well without it. Evaluation is necessary at every step of the development process. Enhance context input into a model by giving the model access to external data sources and tools for information gathering. Put in guardrails to protect your system and your users. Add model router and gateway to support complex pipelines and add more security. Optimize for latency and costs with cache. Add complex logic and write actions to maximize your system’s capabilities. Observability, which allows you to gain visibility into your system for monitoring and debugging, and orchestration, which involves chaining all the components together, are two essential components of the platform. We will discuss them at the end of this post. » What this post is not « This post focuses on the overall architecture for deploying AI applications. It discusses what components are needed and considerations when building these components. It’s not about how to build AI applications and, therefore, does NOT discuss model evaluation, application evaluation, prompt engineering, finetuning, data annotation guidelines, or chunking strategies for RAGs. All these topics are covered in my upcoming book AI Engineering . Step 1. Enhance Context The initial expansion of a platform usually involves adding mechanisms to allow the system to augment each query with the necessary information. Gathering the relevant information is called context construction. Many queries require context to answer. The more relevant information there is in the context, the less the model has to rely on its internal knowledge, which can be unreliable due to its training data and training methodology. Studies have shown that having access to relevant information in the context can help the model generate more detailed responses while reducing hallucinations ( Lewis et al. , 2020). For example, given the query “Will Acme’s fancy-printer-A300 print 100pps?”, the model will be able to respond better if it’s given the specifications of fancy-printer-A300. (Thanks Chetan Tekur for the example.) Context construction for foundation models is equivalent to feature engineering for classical ML models. They serve the same purpose: giving the model the necessary information to process an input. In-context learning, learning from the context, is a form of continual learning. It enables a model to incorporate new information continually to make decisions, preventing it from becoming outdated. For example, a model trained on last-week data won’t be able to answer questions about this week unless the new information is included in its context. By updating a model’s context with the latest information, e.g. fancy-printer-A300’s latest specifications, the model remains up-to-date and can respond to queries beyond its cut-off date. RAGs The most well-known pattern for context construction is RAG, Retrieval-Augmented Generation. RAG consists of two components: a generator (e.g. a language model) and a retriever, which retrieves relevant information from external sources. Retrieval isn’t unique to RAGs. It’s the backbone of search engines, recommender systems, log analytics, etc. Many retrieval algorithms developed for traditional retrieval systems can be used for RAGs. External memory sources typically contain unstructured data, such as memos, contracts, news updates, etc. They can be collectively called documents . A document can be 10 tokens or 1 million tokens. Naively retrieving whole documents can cause your context to be arbitrarily long. RAG typically requires documents to be split into manageable chunks , which can be determined from the model’s maximum context length and your application’s latency requirements. To learn more about chunking and the optimal chunk size, see Pinecone , Langchain , Llamaindex , and Greg Kamradt ’s tutorials. Once data from external memory sources has been loaded and chunked, retrieval is performed using two main approaches. Term-based retrieval This can be as simple as keyword search. For example, given the query “transformer”, fetch all documents containing this keyword. More sophisticated algorithms include BM25 (which leverages TF-IDF) and Elasticsearch (which leverages inverted index). Term-based retrieval is usually used for text data, but it also works for images and videos that have text metadata such as titles, tags, captions, comments, etc. Embedding-based retrieval (also known as vector search) You convert chunks of data into embedding vectors using an embedding model such as BERT , sentence-transformers , and proprietary embedding models provided by OpenAI or Google. Given a query, the data whose vectors are closest to the query embedding, as determined by the vector search algorithm, is retrieved. Vector search is usually framed as nearest-neighbor search, using approximate nearest neighbor (ANN) algorithms such as FAISS (Facebook AI Similarity Search), Google’s ScaNN , Spotify’s ANNOY , and hnswlib ( Hierarchical Navigable Small World ). The ANN-benchmarks website compares different ANN algorithms on multiple datasets using four main metrics, taking into account the tradeoffs between indexing and querying. Recall : the fraction of the nearest neighbors found by the algorithm. Query per second (QPS) : the number of queries the algorithm can handle per second. This is crucial for high-traffic applications. Build time : the time required to build the index. This metric is important especially if you need to frequently update your index (e.g. because your data changes). Index size : the size of the index created by the algorithm, which is crucial for assessing its scalability and storage requirements. This works with not just text documents, but also images, videos, audio, and code. Many teams even try to summarize SQL tables and dataframes and then use these summaries to generate embeddings for retrieval. Term-based retrieval is much faster and cheaper than embedding-based retrieval. It can work well out of the box, making it an attractive option to start. Both BM25 and Elasticsearch are widely used in the industry and serve as formidable baselines for more complex retrieval systems. Embedding-based retrieval, while computationally expensive, can be significantly improved over time to outperform term-based retrieval. A production retrieval system typically combines several approaches. Combining term-based retrieval and embedding-based retrieval is called hybrid search . One common pattern is sequential. First, a cheap, less precise retriever, such as a term-based system, fetches candidates. Then, a more precise but more expensive mechanism, such as k-nearest neighbors, finds the best of these candidates. The second step is also called reranking. For example, given the term “transformer”, you can fetch all documents that contain the word transformer, regardless of whether they are about the electric device, the neural architecture, or the movie. Then you use vector search to find among these documents those that are actually related to your transformer query. Context reranking differs from traditional search reranking in that the exact position of items is less critical. In search, the rank (e.g., first or fifth) is crucial. In context reranking, the order of documents still matters because it affects how well a model can process them. Models might better understand documents at the beginning and end of the context, as suggested by the paper Lost in the middle (Liu et al., 2023). However, as long as a document is included, the impact of its order is less significant compared to in search ranking. Another pattern is ensemble. Remember that a retriever works by ranking documents by their relevance scores to the query. You use multiple retrievers to fetch candidates at the same time, then combine these different rankings together to generate a final ranking. RAGs with tabular data External data sources can also be structured, such as dataframes or SQL tables. Retrieving data from an SQL table is significantly different from retrieving data from unstructured documents. Given a query, the system works as follows. Text-to-SQL : Based on the user query and the table schemas, determine what SQL query is needed. SQL execution : Execute the SQL query. Generation : Generate a response based on the SQL result and the original user query. For the text-to-SQL step, if there are many available tables whose schemas can’t all fit into the model context, you might need an intermediate step to predict what tables to use for each query. Text-to-SQL can be done by the same model used to generate the final response or one of many specialized text-to-SQL models. Agentic RAGs An important source of data is the Internet. A web search tool like Google or Bing API can give the model access to a rich, up-to-date resource to gather relevant information for each query. For example, given the query “Who won Oscar this year?”, the system searches for information about the latest Oscar and uses this information to generate the final response to the user. Term-based retrieval, embedding-based retrieval, SQL execution, and web search are actions that a model can take to augment its context. You can think of each action as a function the model can call. A workflow that can incorporate external actions is also called agentic . The architecture then looks like this. » Action vs. tool « A tool allows one or more actions. For example, a people search tool might allow two actions: search by name and search by email. However, the difference is minimal, so many people use action and tool interchangeably. » Read-only actions vs. write actions « Actions that retrieve information from external sources but don’t change their states are read-only actions. Giving a model write actions, e.g. updating the values in a table, enables the model to perform more tasks but also poses more risks, which will be discussed later. Query rewriting Often, a user query needs to be rewritten to increase the likelihood of fetching the right information. Consider the following conversation. User: When was the last time John Doe bought something from us? AI: John last bought a Fruity Fedora hat from us two weeks ago, on January 3, 2030. User: How about Emily Doe? The last question, “How about Emily Doe?”, is ambiguous. If you use this query verbatim to retrieve documents, you’ll likely get irrelevant results. You need to rewrite this query to reflect what the user is actually asking. The new query should make sense on its own. The last question should be rewritten to “When was the last time Emily Doe bought something from us?” Query rewriting is typically done using other AI models, using a prompt similar to “Given the following conversation, rewrite the last user input to reflect what the user is actually asking.” Query rewriting can get complicated, especially if you need to do identity resolution or incorporate other knowledge. If the user asks “How about his wife?”, you will first need to query your database to find out who his wife is. If you don’t have this information, the rewriting model should acknowledge that this query isn’t solvable instead of hallucinating a name, leading to a wrong answer. Step 2. Put in Guardrails Guardrails help reduce AI risks and protect not just your users but also you, the developers. They should be placed whenever there is potential for failures. This post discusses two types of guardrails: input guardrails and output guardrails. Input guardrails Input guardrails are typically protection against two types of risks: leaking private information to external APIs, and executing bad prompts that compromise your system (model jailbreaking). Leaking private information to external APIs This risk is specific to using external model APIs when you need to send your data outside your organization. For example, an employee might copy the company’s secret or a user’s private information into a prompt and send it to wherever the model is hosted. One of the most notable early incidents was when Samsung employees put Samsung’s proprietary information into ChatGPT, accidentally leaking the company’s secrets . It’s unclear how Samsung discovered this leak and how the leaked information was used against Samsung. However, the incident was serious enough for Samsung to ban ChatGPT in May 2023 . There’s no airtight way to eliminate potential leaks when using third-party APIs. However, you can mitigate them with guardrails. You can use one of the many available tools that automatically detect sensitive data. What sensitive data to detect is specified by you. Common sensitive data classes are: Personal information (ID numbers, phone numbers, bank accounts). Human faces. Specific keywords and phrases associated with the company’s intellectual properties or privileged information. Many sensitive data detection tools use AI to identify potentially sensitive information, such as determining if a string resembles a valid home address. If a query is found to contain sensitive information, you have two options: block the entire query or remove the sensitive information from it. For instance, you can mask a user’s phone number with the placeholder [PHONE NUMBER]. If the generated response contains this placeholder, use a PII reversible dictionary that maps this placeholder to the original information so that you can unmask it, as shown below. Model jailbreaking It’s become an online sport to try to jailbreak AI models, getting them to say or do bad things. While some might find it amusing to get ChatGPT to make controversial statements, it’s much less fun if your customer support chatbot, branded with your name and logo, does the same thing. This can be especially dangerous for AI systems that have access to tools. Imagine if a user finds a way to get your system to execute an SQL query that corrupts your data. To combat this, you should first put guardrails on your system so that no harmful actions can be automatically executed. For example, no SQL queries that can insert, delete, or update data can be executed without human approval. The downside of this added security is that it can slow down your system. To prevent your application from making outrageous statements it shouldn’t be making, you can define out-of-scope topics for your application. For example, if your application is a customer support chatbot, it shouldn’t answer political or social questions. A simple way to do so is to filter out inputs that contain predefined phrases typically associated with controversial topics, such as “immigration” or “antivax”. More sophisticated algorithms use AI to classify whether an input is about one of the pre-defined restricted topics. If harmful prompts are rare in your system, you can use an anomaly detection algorithm to identify unusual prompts. Output guardrails AI models are probabilistic, making their outputs unreliable. You can put in guardrails to significantly improve your application’s reliability. Output guardrails have two main functionalities: Evaluate the quality of each generation. Specify the policy to deal with different failure modes. Output quality measurement To catch outputs that fail to meet your standards, you need to understand what failures look like. Here are examples of failure modes and how to catch them. Empty responses . Malformatted responses that don’t follow the expected output format. For example, if the application expects JSON and the generated response has a missing closing bracket. There are validators for certain formats, such as regex, JSON, and Python code validators. There are also tools for constrained sampling such as guidance, outlines, and instructor. Toxic responses , such as those that are racist or sexist. These responses can be caught using one of many toxicity detection tools. Factual inconsistent responses hallucinated by the model. Hallucination detection is an active area of research with solutions such as SelfCheckGPT (Manakul et al., 2023) and SAFE , Search Engine Factuality Evaluator (Wei et al., 2024). You can mitigate hallucinations by providing models with sufficient context and prompting techniques such as chain-of-thought. Hallucination detection and mitigation are discussed further in my upcoming book AI Engineering . Responses that contain sensitive information . This can happen in two scenarios. Your model was trained on sensitive data and regurgitates it back. Your system retrieves sensitive information from your internal database to enrich its context, and then it passes this sensitive information on to the response. This failure mode can be prevented by not training your model on sensitive data and not allowing it to retrieve sensitive data in the first place. Sensitive data in outputs can be detected using the same tools used for input guardrails. Brand-risk responses , such as responses that mischaracterize your company or your competitors. An example is when Grok, a model trained by X, generated a response suggesting that Grok was trained by OpenAI , causing the Internet to suspect X of stealing OpenAI’s data. This failure mode can be mitigated with keyword monitoring. Once you’ve identified outputs concerning your brands and competitors, you can either block these outputs, pass them onto human reviewers, or use other models to detect the sentiment of these outputs to ensure that only the right sentiments are returned. Generally bad responses . For example, if you ask the model to write an essay and that essay is just bad, or if you ask the model for a low-calorie cake recipe and the generated recipe contains an excessive amount of sugar. It’s become a popular practice to use AI judges to evaluate the quality of models’ responses. These AI judges can be general-purpose models (think ChatGPT, Claude) or specialized scorers trained to output a concrete score for a response given a query. Failure management AI models are probabilistic, which means that if you try a query again, you might get a different response. Many failures can be mitigated using a basic retry logic. For example, if the response is empty, try again X times or until you get a non-empty response. Similarly, if the response is malformatted, try again until the model generates a correctly formatted response. This retry policy, however, can incur extra latency and cost. One retry means 2x the number of API calls. If the retry is carried out after failure, the latency experienced by the user will double. To reduce latency, you can make calls in parallel. For example, for each query, instead of waiting for the first query to fail before retrying, you send this query to the model twice at the same time, get back two responses, and pick the better one. This increases the number of redundant API calls but keeps latency manageable. It’s also common to fall back on humans to handle tricky queries. For example, you can transfer a query to human operators if it contains specific key phrases. Some teams use a specialized model, potentially trained in-house, to decide when to transfer a conversation to humans. One team, for instance, transfers a conversation to human operators when their sentiment analysis model detects that the user is getting angry. Another team transfers a conversation after a certain number of turns to prevent users from getting stuck in an infinite loop. Guardrail tradeoffs Reliability vs. latency tradeoff : While acknowledging the importance of guardrails, some teams told me that latency is more important. They decided not to implement guardrails because they can significantly increase their application’s latency. However, these teams are in the minority. Most teams find that the increased risks are more costly than the added latency. Output guardrails might not work well in the stream completion mode. By default, the whole response is generated before shown to the user, which can take a long time. In the stream completion mode, new tokens are streamed to the user as they are generated, reducing the time the user has to wait to see the response. The downside is that it’s hard to evaluate partial responses, so unsafe responses might be streamed to users before the system guardrails can determine that they should be blocked. Self-hosted vs. third-party API tradeoff : Self-hosting your models means that you don’t have to send your data to a third party, reducing the need for input guardrails. However, it also means that you must implement all the necessary guardrails yourself, rather than relying on the guardrails provided by third-party services. Our platform now looks like this.
